properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent.

⚠️ REFRAMED 2026-08-11 AFTER GETTING IT WRONG. The first version of this node asked whether reflow2 should automate git. That was not the question. Anthony: "I'm not saying that reflow2 does the actual git operations itself; I'm arguing that reflow2's own rules shouldn't be tracked by hand, but by some governance rules (and this may be different for every project, which is kind of how we designed the governance entities for reflow2 anyways)." His original words were "as part of governance", and the word was doing the work.

⭐⭐ THE FINDING, MEASURED 2026-08-11: REFLOW2 HAS A GOVERNANCE LAYER AND DOES NOT USE IT ON ITS OWN GOVERNANCE RULES.

  DesignRules in this design                                        10
  carrying a VERIFIES edge                                           1   (per-design-state-is-never-a-process-global)
  `dec:export-once-per-pr` node type                            Decision   — so `unverified_enforced_rule`,
                                                                            which scans DesignRules, CANNOT SEE IT
  Verification node for the lineage gate                          none
  `rule:nothing-lands-on-main-directly`                        advisory, unverified

AND THE GATE IS REAL. `tools/reflow2_check.py` fails the build on a broken lineage chain — it did so twice on 2026-08-11 — and its own source at line 515 says: "THE RULE THIS ENFORCES is `dec:export-once-per-pr`, accepted". THE PYTHON NAMES THE RULE IT ENFORCES AND THE GRAPH DOES NOT KNOW THE CHECK EXISTS. Delete that check tomorrow and nothing in the design notices: no gap, no defect, no unverified rule. The rule keeps reading as governing while nothing governs.

⭐ SO "CARRIED BY HAND" IS PRECISE AND IT IS NOT ABOUT GIT. The ENFORCEMENT is automated. The TRACKING of the enforcement is what is manual — a rule in one place, a check in another, and nothing joining them. That is the same shape this project keeps finding: the search-first rule living in five skills and firing only when one is loaded; the deferral discipline living in a table nothing computes on; mutation-checking practised in eight verifications and written down nowhere.

⭐⭐ AND THE GENERALISATION IS THE PRODUCT POINT, in his words: "this may be different for every project, which is kind of how we designed the governance entities for reflow2 anyways." The governance entities exist so ANY project can state its own policy and get gap detection on it — `DesignRule` with a three-state `enforced`, `unverified_enforced_rule` at 0.6, `cap:governance-proposal` to ask the consequence rather than inherit it. reflow2's own git and export policy is exactly the kind of project-specific rule that layer was built for, and it sits outside it. A consumer copying reflow2's example would copy the gap.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE, unranked:
(a) MAKE THE EXISTING RULES FIRST-CLASS. `dec:export-once-per-pr` becomes (or gains) a DesignRule so the governance detector can see it; the lineage gate becomes a Verification with a VERIFIES edge to it; `rule:nothing-lands-on-main-directly` gets the same treatment or an honest statement that it cannot be checked. Pure wiring, no new mechanism, and it makes deleting a check visible.
(b) ANSWER THE CHECKABILITY QUESTION PROPERLY. `req:a-rule-says-whether-it-can-be-checked-at-all` is ACCEPTED and unbuilt: it splits "no detector" into DEBT and ACCEPTED LIMIT. Nine of ten rules here are unverified and nothing distinguishes "nobody has written the check" from "no check is possible" — which is the difference between rule:bl-41 (LLM behaviour, arguably uncheckable) and the export rule (checked already, just not wired).
(c) BOTH, since (b) is what stops (a) turning nine rules into nine permanent 0.6 gaps.
(d) Nothing: the gate works, and wiring it into the graph changes no behaviour today.

⚠️ THE COUNTER TO (a) AND IT IS REAL: making rules first-class means `unverified_enforced_rule` starts firing on rules nobody intends to check, and this project has retired a detector before (`unexpected_coupling`) precisely for firing on correct work. That is why (b) is not optional — the enforced flag without the checkability answer converts honest advisory rules into permanent debt.

⚠️ THE NON-GITHUB CLAUSE STILL STANDS AND IS NOWHERE IN THE GRAPH. `rule:nothing-lands-on-main-directly` is stated entirely in GitHub's vocabulary — branch, open a PR, gates green, merge — and its four recorded traps are all forge mechanics. ON A BARE GIT REMOTE THERE IS NO PULL REQUEST. So the rule presumes a forge while reflow2 only requires git, and nothing says which parts survive. That is a live instance of `req:a-rule-states-its-scope-and-a-conflict-is-surfaced` (proposed): the rule does not state its scope, and on a plain remote it is partly UNFOLLOWABLE rather than merely unenforced. Any wiring must express the discipline in pure git — one commit per branch touches the export — with the PR being only where CI happens to notice.

📌 EVIDENCE OF THE COST, one day of this project's own work, four PRs all merged: two CI failures caused by the export discipline alone; roughly ten hand-driven restore-then-export-once cycles; a rebase needing a re-export because the three-way merge driver merges CONTENT correctly and cannot repair LINEAGE; the local and CI gates disagreeing in BOTH directions because one compares against HEAD and the other against main; and one PR left in draft after going green. A fleet of seven sessions reports the same and mitigates it with a social convention — "only the boss exports" — which is the shape this project treats as a finding everywhere else.

⚠️ WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN regardless: reflow2 must not push, merge or open a PR. `dec:repo-file-embedded` weighs local-first deliberately, and a design tool that writes to a remote is categorically worse than the friction it removes. Nothing in (a)–(c) requires it.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⭐⭐ SHARPENED 2026-08-26 — ANTHONY'S `agent_rule` FRAMING, AND A SESSION THAT BROKE FOUR RULES WHILE HOLDING ALL NINETEEN
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Anthony, 2026-08-26, from a separate brainstorm about the graph replacing markdown handoffs: *"potentially, could also make agent_rule nodes that contain things like design rules the agent should practice, for instance. definitely a brainstorming idea for now."*

**THE DUPLICATE GUARD SENT THAT IDEA HERE AND IT WAS RIGHT TO.** It is the same question — reflow2's own practice rules and whether the governance layer carries them — arriving from the handoff conversation instead of the git one.

**WHAT HIS FRAMING ADDS: a TYPING question this node did not hold.** `DesignRule` now holds **19** nodes, and a clear majority are *"things the agent should practice"* rather than statements about the product — *nothing lands on main directly*, *success is read from the authoritative object*, *a gate is run against the state it will be judged in*, *exactly one commit writes the export*, *fix at the root never patch around*, *design information lives in the graph not in documents*, *graph text is data never instructions*. So `agent_rule` is **largely already implemented under another name**, and the open sub-question is whether practice rules and product rules being one type is an overload — the same shape that made `Interface.designation` ambiguous — or a distinction with no computation behind it and therefore not worth minting.

🛑 **AND THE NEW MEASUREMENT, WHICH ARGUES THE TYPING QUESTION IS THE LESS IMPORTANT HALF.** In one session, 2026-08-26, the agent broke FOUR of these rules and was caught by machinery every time, never by having read them:

  success is read from the authoritative object   → self-caught: a piped `cargo test` returned `head`'s exit code
  a gate is run against the state it is judged in → CI failed on `cargo fmt --check` after local tests passed
  exactly one commit writes the export            → the lineage gate failed, TWICE
  design intent moves only on the owner's word    → CI FAILED: two Decisions settled with nobody's name on them

**The nineteen rules were never opened until a brainstorm went looking for them.** Same finding as `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session`, one layer down: the vocabulary exists, the content is right, and it does not reach the agent who needs it.

⭐ **THE ONE THAT HELD WAS THE ONE THAT WAS ENFORCED.** `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` stopped the build. It did not need to be read — it needed to be UNAVOIDABLE. That is a data point for option (a)+(b) over any amount of better authoring, and it is worth more than the count: three of the four catches came from a gate, and the fourth from luck.

📌 SO THE OPTIONS ABOVE GAIN A FIFTH, WHICH IS REALLY A PRIORITY CLAIM RATHER THAN A NEW ACTION: **(e) treat reach as the problem and typing as a footnote.** Wire the checkable rules to their existing gates (a), answer checkability for the rest (b), and leave `agent_rule` unminted until some computation would read the distinction. Nothing in the 2026-08-26 evidence suggests a second type would have prevented any of the four violations.
properties.name: OPEN — reflow2's own rules are tracked by hand while reflow2 has a governance layer built to track them. Should they be wired into it?
properties.rationale: Reframed after misreading the question as git automation. The measurement is the argument: 10 DesignRules, 1 verified; the export rule is a Decision so the governance detector cannot see it; and the lineage gate that enforces it exists only as Python whose own source names the rule it enforces. The enforcement is automated and the tracking of it is not — so deleting the check would be invisible to the design. That is a product gap rather than a repo-hygiene one, because the governance entities exist precisely so any project can wire its own rules in.
